summary: The OpenCode coding agent, driven in a terminal.

manual.$comment: OpenCode takes no flag for this, but its configuration takes a permission rule set, merged over the person's own, and the last matching rule wins: the wildcard comes first and every tool OpenCode names follows it. Reads, searches and listings run; edits, commands, the web and anything outside the project ask. The same rule set a chat gets. Told twice: 1.x reads OPENCODE_PERMISSION; 2.x no longer does (absent from the 2.0.32 binary, and a Manual chat there ran a shell command unasked) but reads `permission` from OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT, which 1.x reads too, and maps `bash` and `task` onto its `shell` and `subagent`. Measured live against 1.18.32 and 2.0.32 on 2026-10-17. The document joins the host context's instructions and the launch integration's tables rather than replacing them (mergeJsonEnv).
manual.label: Ask
manual.description: OpenCode permission rules that ask before every edit, command and web request. Reading, searching and listing the project does not ask.

auto.$comment: The manual rule set with edits allowed.
auto.label: Allow edits
auto.description: OpenCode permission rules that let file edits in the project through and ask before commands, web requests and anything outside the project.

bypass.$comment: OpenCode has exactly ONE permission flag. `opencode --help` documents `--auto` ("auto-approve permissions that are not explicitly denied (dangerous!)") and nothing else — there is no `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which is what this preset used to send. OpenCode's parser is not strict, so the unknown flag was silently dropped: choosing Bypass did nothing and the session kept prompting, with no error anywhere.
bypass.label: Auto-approve
bypass.description: OpenCode’s --auto: every permission your rules do not explicitly deny is approved. Use only in repositories you trust.

none.label: Your rules
none.description: Pass no permission rules, so your own OpenCode configuration decides what asks.

overflow.$comment: `opencode run` is a one-shot command, not a TUI, so there is no composer to type an overflowed message into. `opencode run --help` (1.18.30) documents `-f, --file` ("file(s) to attach to message"), so a first message too long for the platform's command line is written to a file and attached, and `{{prompt}}` renders a one-line note naming it. The note comes first because -f is an array option: a positional after it would be read as another file. Not verified end to end: this machine has no provider credentials.

contextInjection.$comment: OpenCode has no system-prompt flag; it merges OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT (JSON) over the config it already loaded, and `instructions` is a list of instruction FILES. Verified against the installed binary, which reads process.env.OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT and merges it last. Env rather than argv, so a resumed session is re-told for free. The path goes in as {{contextFileJson}} — a JSON string literal — because a Windows path's backslashes would otherwise be JSON escapes and the config would not parse. A user who already exports OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT is merged with rather than clobbered — see mergeProviderLaunchEnv in terminal-launch.ts.

launchIntegration.$comment: The agent-state plugin (by file:// URL), the MCP table and a launch skill's folder (skills.paths) in OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT, merged with the host context's instructions. Measured against opencode 1.18.32 on 2026-10-16: a plugin named by URL loads beside the person's own with nothing installed next to it, `mcp` merges field by field and wins on the same id, and skills.paths folders are scanned for SKILL.md.

installTargets.$comment: restartRequired NOT verified on 2026-07-29: OpenCode has no local skill picker to observe (skills are invoked by mention), and this machine has no provider credentials, so a model turn could not be run to test it. Left true — a banner that over-warns is recoverable, one that under-warns is not.

agentStateSpec.$comment: OpenCode has no command-hook mechanism; it auto-loads in-process JS plugins from .opencode/plugin/ and exposes a typed event stream, so the reporter is the named bundled plugin TEMPLATE with the socket path baked in at install (dest is .js because OpenCode's loader ignores .mjs, verified against v1.17.11, still true on 1.18.30). The events table below is the canonical event→phase mapping the main process applies to each frame; the plugin's internal copy only decides what it reports and dedups on. message.updated is the working signal (no discrete thinking-start event exists); permission.replied → thinking is load-bearing — it is the only signal that clears awaiting_input after the user answers a prompt; session.error maps to idle WITH failure:true because a crashed session must not read as a clean turn end; no event maps to exited — a real process exit is owned by the pty exit listener. register flags are meaningless here (the plugin subscribes itself). Agent changelists: OpenCode calls the plugin's `tool.execute.after` with the call INPUT ({tool, sessionID, callID, args}) and the tool RESULT ({title, output, metadata}) as two arguments, and a tool that threw never reaches it. VERIFIED live against opencode 1.18.30, the latest release (2026-09-09): `edit` carries output.metadata.filediff {file (ABSOLUTE), patch, additions, deletions} plus the same text as metadata.diff — a real unified diff (jsdiff formatPatch: Index:/===/---/+++ headers, 4 context lines), so the plugin walks the patch text for HUNK-LEVEL ranges; `write` carries NO diff at all, only metadata.filepath + metadata.exists, so a write that CREATED the file is counted from args.content as one `-0,0 +1,N` region and an overwrite is a file-level claim (path, 0/0, no edits). `apply_patch` carries metadata.files [{filePath, relativePath, type, patch, additions, deletions, movePath?}] and is read for ONE FRAME PER FILE — that shape is from the shipped binary, not a live run: apply_patch is an OpenAI-provider tool and was not registered for the model the capture ran on. The `file.edited` event ({file} only) is DELIBERATELY not subscribed: it is published by these same three tools and carries no line ranges, so a frame from it would be a path-only claim that recordEdit treats as a no-op on an owned file and as the same whole-file claim on an unowned one — one extra socket write per edit for nothing. Paths are resolved against the plugin context's `directory` because `relativePath` is relative to the worktree.

selfUpdate.$comment: Verified 2026-10-13 against OpenCode 1.18.32: `opencode upgrade --help` documents `upgrade [target]` and `--method` (curl, npm, pnpm, bun, brew, choco, scoop). Without `--method` it works out the method itself, `curl` for a binary under ~/.opencode/bin, which is where the install script puts it. For a binary it cannot place it asks ("Install anyways?") before going on, which is why this runs only for a binary under neither Homebrew nor npm (chooseCliUpdateCommand); a Homebrew or npm install is updated by its own manager.

capabilities.$comment: resumeSession is intentionally false: OpenCode's resume (opencode run --continue --session {{sessionId}}) is structurally caller-independent like Codex and very likely works, but it was excluded as unverified and real-app OpenCode resume is not drivable headless. false = zero behavior change vs. today. Flip to true (no code change) once resume is verified end-to-end to preserve the conversation.
